section.title: The Greatness of Mordecai
section.sectionRationale: The book closes with three quiet verses that seal the reversal. The king who once signed a death warrant for the Jews now taxes the empire in peace; Mordecai, once sitting in sackcloth at the gate, is second only to the king, his deeds written in the royal chronicles. The final word is not about power for its own sake but about a man who used his greatness to seek the good of his people and to speak peace to all his kindred. The exiled Jew has become a blessing at the heart of a pagan empire.
section.thesis: The book ends not with a miracle but with a man raised high who bends his greatness to the good and peace of his people, a faint and faithful shadow of the greater Deliverer to come.
section.frameNote: One movement: the empire at peace, Mordecai exalted second to the king, and his greatness spent seeking the good and peace of his people.

units.label: The greatness of Mordecai
units.note: power bent to the good of the people

verses.text: Now King Xerxes imposed tribute throughout the land, even to its farthest shores.

And all of Mordecai’s powerful and magnificent accomplishments, together with the full account of the {{gedullah|greatness}} to which the king had raised him, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia?

For Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes, preeminent among the Jews and highly favored by his many kinsmen, seeking the {{tov|good}} of his people and speaking {{shalom|peace}} to all his countrymen.

gedullah.gloss: Greatness, high rank, magnificence. The word recalls the very honor Haman once craved and paraded, now given instead to Mordecai. In a book of reversals, the greatness the proud enemy sought for himself lands on the faithful servant, and the closing chronicle records not a self-made rise but a greatness to which the king raised him.

tov.gloss: Good, welfare, benefit. Mordecai's greatness is defined by what he does with it: he seeks the tov, the good, of his people. The word measures true greatness not by how high a man is lifted but by whose welfare he pursues, and it marks Mordecai as a ruler after the pattern of the God who works all things for the good of His people.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, well-being. The book that opened with a death sentence closes with a man speaking shalom to all his kindred. The word is the great biblical sign of God's saving order, and Mordecai the peace-speaker is a small foreshadowing of the Prince of Peace, who secures a wholeness his exiled forebears could only glimpse.

basic.context: The book ends with a short, calm epilogue. The same king who once let the Jews be marked for death now rules a settled empire, collecting taxes in peace. Mordecai, who began the story sitting at the gate and later sat in sackcloth and ashes, is now second only to the king, his deeds recorded in the royal chronicles. But the last word is not simply that he became powerful. It is that he used his power well, seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his fellow Jews. The exile has become a blessing at the center of a foreign empire.
basic.hermeneutics: These three verses are a deliberate, understated close. The key question is what kind of greatness the book wants us to admire. The answer comes in the final line: greatness measured not by rank but by seeking the good and peace of others. A further question is why the book ends here, with an earthly Jew great in Persia, and not with a return to Jerusalem or a word from God. The lesson is that God can raise His servants to bless His people even in exile, and that true greatness serves.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter turns on three words. Mordecai is raised to gedullah, greatness, the very honor Haman once craved for himself. But his greatness is defined by tov, the good he seeks for his people, and by shalom, the peace he speaks to all his kindred. The book that opened with a decree of death closes with a great man spending his greatness on the good and peace of others.
basic.typology: Mordecai, the once-lowly Jew raised to be second in the kingdom and using his power to save and bless his people, foreshadows Christ, exalted to the right hand of God, who seeks the good and speaks the peace of His people. Mordecai's rescue was partial and earthly; Christ's is complete and eternal.
basic.christ: Mordecai's greatness is a faint shadow of a greater exaltation. He was lifted to second in the empire and used his position to seek the good and peace of his people; Christ was lifted to the highest place and secures the eternal good and peace of His people. Mordecai was a man of the moment used by God; Jesus is God Himself come to deliver forever, the true peace-speaker.
basic.god: God is not named even in the final verse, and the book ends without a return to the promised land or a voice from heaven. Yet the whole close testifies to Him: the exile is not abandoned, a faithful servant is raised, and God's people are cared for far from home. The hidden God who ruled a sleepless night now rules the settled peace of an empire, working the good of His people through a man He has exalted.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 41 shows Joseph raised to second in Egypt to save his people, the pattern Mordecai follows. Jeremiah 29 tells the exiles to seek the peace of the city where God has sent them. Philippians 2 exalts the humbled Christ to the highest place. And Isaiah 9 names Him the Prince of Peace.
basic.oneStory: The book ends with an exiled Jew raised to greatness and spending it on the good and peace of his people, a quiet echo of Joseph and a faint foreshadowing of Christ. Mordecai's deliverance was partial and passing; the true Deliverer, exalted forever, secures the everlasting good and peace of all God's people.

context.literary:
These three verses close the book with a formula borrowed from another kind of book. The question 'are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles?' in 10:2 is the closing line the historian of Kings uses for the reigns of Israel's and Judah's rulers, for example 1 Kings 11:41 and 14:19. Esther ends by giving Mordecai a royal obituary notice, and it points to the archives of Media and Persia instead of the archives of Israel. The exile has moved the centre of the story from the temple to a foreign court, and the book's last formal act is to write a Jew into the chronicle of a pagan crown.

That chronicle has been a running motif. In 2:23 Mordecai's rescue of the king was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles and then forgotten. In 6:1 a sleepless king had the same book read to him, and Mordecai's deed was found unrewarded. Here, at the end, the book has finished paying the debt: what was once an unrewarded entry is now a whole 'account of the greatness' to which the king raised him. The writer closes a loop that has been open since chapter 2.

There is also a deliberate echo with chapter 1. The book opened with Xerxes displaying 'the magnificent splendor of his greatness,' 1:4, and the Hebrew there uses the two nouns for honor and greatness that fall, in this chapter and in 8:16, on the Jews. The honor that belonged to the king's display now belongs to a Jewish courtier, and the greatness the book began by admiring in a king it ends by admiring in a servant.

Inside the three verses the movement is compact. Verse 1 fixes the king and his empire. Verse 2 turns to Mordecai's record. Verse 3 begins with the word 'for' and supplies the reason for everything before it: he was second to the king, great among the Jews, well received by his kinsmen, and, in the last two clauses, he sought his people's good and spoke peace to every one of his own descendants. The last word of the Hebrew is the word for seed or offspring.
context.historical:
Xerxes' tribute in 10:1 fits what is known of his reign. He ruled from about 486 to 465 BC and depended on the empire's revenue for his building projects at Persepolis and Susa and for his campaigns in the west. The book has already placed these events in his twelfth year, 3:7, some years after the failed invasion of Greece, and the mention of tribute on the land and the coastlands is a small note of realism: the empire went on collecting what it always collected. The Jews' reprieve did not change the machine of the state; it changed their place in it.

The king in this chapter is the same king. He is not portrayed as reformed or converted. That is why the last verse is about Mordecai, and why the historical situation matters. A dispersed people living under a foreign crown depended on the good will of people at court, and the book of Esther is one of three Old Testament stories of Jews who rose high in a foreign administration, alongside Daniel in Babylon and Persia, Daniel 2:48, and Nehemiah as the king's cupbearer, Nehemiah 2:1. Other evidence shows Jewish communities living quietly in the Persian empire: the papyri from Elephantine in Egypt come from a Jewish garrison town of that century.

The phrase 'second only to King Xerxes' names a real office in the ancient court. The same expression is used of a court official in 2 Chronicles 28:7, and Pharaoh's second chariot for Joseph, Genesis 41:43, uses the same root. Mordecai holds the office Haman once held, the prime minister's seat in the Persian government.

Finally, the Hebrew text ends here with no mention of Jerusalem. Later Greek versions of Esther add material that names God and includes an interpreted dream of Mordecai. The shorter Hebrew ending is the one the Protestant Old Testament preserves, and the closing silence is part of what the book asks its readers to hear.
context.canonical:
Mordecai's closing portrait stands in a line of exiles who prospered in a foreign court to bless their own people. The obvious ancestor is Joseph, who was given the ring, the robes and the second chariot, Genesis 41:42-43, and said to be second only to Pharaoh's throne, Genesis 41:40. The obvious pastoral counterpart is Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, which tells them to seek the prosperity of the city to which they were sent and to pray for it, Jeremiah 29:7. Mordecai does what Jeremiah told the exiles to do and, unlike most of them, has the office to do it well.

The phrase 'seeking the good' and 'speaking peace' also has old roots. Psalm 122:8-9 says 'for the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, Peace be within you,' and 'I will seek your prosperity.' Psalm 85:8 says God Himself 'will surely speak peace to His people.' Deuteronomy 23:6 tells Israel not to 'seek peace or prosperity' for two hostile neighbours, so that the Torah's own language for what a nation owes its friends and its enemies is being applied here to Mordecai's care of his own.

The New Testament carries the themes forward in two ways. Jesus takes the idea of greatness and overturns it: 'whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,' Matthew 20:26, and the Son of Man 'did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Matthew 20:28. And the writers of the New Testament take the ideas of peace spoken to the far and the near, Ephesians 2:17, and the Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6, as titles of Christ, who is the peace Mordecai's speech only pointed toward.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author is giving the community a model and a limit at the same moment. The model is Mordecai: a man raised to the top of a system that owed him nothing who chose to use his position for the good of others and to speak peace, not to settle scores. The final verse says nothing about what he did to his enemies, though he had every power to do it. It says what he sought and what he spoke.

The limit is the book's refusal to close the story with more than a good man in a foreign court. There is no return to Jerusalem, no temple, no prophecy and no voice from heaven. A community in exile is told that a faithful life inside a foreign empire is a worthy life, that God's care for His people does not depend on a homeland, and that the greatness worth wanting is a greatness spent for others.

The author also means the end to answer the beginning. The book opened on a king who displayed himself, whose word could not be changed and whose courtiers played games with law and appetite. It closes on a servant whose greatness is defined by what he does for others. The ending is a quiet argument about what power is for.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what Mordecai became and what he did with it. It does not command every believer to pursue high office, and it should not be used to bless careerism or political ambition. Mordecai's rise came through a chain of events he did not plan, and the book carefully credits circumstance, not scheming.

What the passage does commend is a habit of heart: seeking the good of one's people and speaking peace to all one's kin. That holds for anyone who has influence of any kind, in a household, a congregation or a workplace. Nor does it suggest that power exercised on behalf of God's people is automatically pure; the book's earlier chapters show Mordecai using the machinery of the state in ways a later reader may find uncomfortable.

The pattern is also plainly under the authority of Jesus' correction. When Christians ask what greatness is, they turn to Matthew 20:25-28 and to Jesus' own servant-hood, and the measure is service, not rank. Mordecai's example remains useful because, at the end of his story, he points the same way.

debates.question: Is Mordecai's final greatness a model to imitate or a caution about the limits of worldly success?

views.label: An exemplar of faithful influence in exile
views.case: The narrator's praise is warm and unqualified. Mordecai is second to the king, favored by his kinsmen and devoted to their good and peace. He fulfils what Jeremiah told the exiles to do, Jeremiah 29:7, and he stands beside Joseph and Daniel as evidence that God can place His servants in centres of power for the sake of others.

views.label: A sober note that earthly greatness is provisional
views.case: Others point to the book's silence about Jerusalem, the temple and God. Mordecai's greatness is recorded in Persia's chronicles, not in Israel's, and it depends on a king who signed the first decree without a second thought. The ending is honest and hopeful, but it leaves the reader looking for a greater deliverer and a better home.

debates.bearing: The two readings can be held together. The verse commends what Mordecai did with power, and the book's setting shows that no human office, however faithfully held, can finish the work of salvation.

debates.question: What does 'well received by the multitude of his brothers' imply about the whole community?

views.label: Broad and genuine approval
views.case: The phrase is a warm summary of a leader who was loved by his people, and the BSB's 'highly favored by his many kinsmen' gives it the plainest sense. Together with the parallel clauses about seeking good and speaking peace, it depicts a man trusted by the community he served.

views.label: Most, though not all, of his brothers
views.case: The Hebrew says most of his brothers, and some readers in the rabbinic tradition took this to mean that a portion of the community was less than pleased, perhaps because his service to Persia cost him time for other duties. On this reading the book realistically admits that even good leadership is not universally welcomed.

debates.bearing: Either way, the narrator is careful to name Mordecai's approval by his own people as part of his greatness. The reader is left to see that a leader worth following is measured by the trust of those he serves, not by a unanimous vote.

study.originalLanguages:
The Hebrew of these verses is compact and a few of its words repay attention. Start with the verb behind the king's promotion in 10:2. The account of Mordecai's greatness is described as the greatness to which the king 'raised him,' and the verb means made great, from the same root as gedullah. This is the verb used of Haman in 3:1, where the king exalted him above all the princes, and in Haman's boast in 5:11, when he told his friends how the king had promoted him. The book uses one word for the elevation of both men. The difference is not in what the king did but in what each man did afterwards.

The opening verse says the king laid a mas on the land and the coastlands. The word means tribute or forced levy, and it is the term used for the labour gangs Solomon raised, 1 Kings 9:15. The word for the far shores means literally the islands or coastlands of the sea, the phrase the prophets use of the distant nations, as in Isaiah 42:4. The king's dominion reaches even to them.

The phrase second only to the king uses mishneh, meaning the second, or the one who stands next. It occurs in the description of an official in 2 Chronicles 28:7 and in the second chariot of Joseph, Genesis 41:43.

The two participles that close the book are the most striking. Mordecai is 'seeking' the good of his people. The verb is darash, a verb most often used in Scripture for seeking the LORD, and it is the verb Jeremiah 29:7 uses when he tells the exiles to seek the peace of Babylon. Set against it is the verb of the enemies of 9:2, who sought to harm the Jews, a different Hebrew verb for seeking. Mordecai seeks for others what his enemies sought against them. He also 'speaks' peace, using the ordinary verb of speech in a way that recalls Psalm 85:8, where God Himself speaks peace to His people, and Psalm 122:8, where a pilgrim says, Peace be within you. The two words tov and shalom occur together in Deuteronomy 23:6, where Israel is forbidden to seek them for Ammon and Moab, so that the pair is the Torah's own vocabulary for what a community owes those it loves.

The last Hebrew word in the book is the word for seed or offspring, translated 'countrymen.' It is the word of the promise to Abraham, Genesis 12:7, and of the promise in Genesis 3:15. The book ends by saying that peace is spoken to all his seed.

typology.type: Mordecai raised from the gate to the second seat, Esther 10:3
typology.fulfillment: A man who sat at a gate in sackcloth is raised to be second to the king, and the elevation follows his people's rescue. The pattern is the exaltation of Christ, who humbled Himself to death on a cross and was raised 'to the highest place,' Philippians 2:9, seated at the right hand of the Father, Acts 2:33. Mordecai's seat was granted by a king who could remove him. Christ's is held by right, and Mordecai's rank was second while Christ's is 'above every name.' The type is faint but true, and it falls short chiefly in that Mordecai was himself in need of the deliverance he helped bring.

typology.type: Seeking the good and speaking peace to all his seed
typology.fulfillment: The last line of the book is a description of a mediator: someone with authority who uses it to secure the good of his people and to speak peace to all of them. Christ is the fulfilment. He 'came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' Ephesians 2:17, and He says, 'Peace I leave with you,' John 14:27. Mordecai's peace was political and for one people, and it lasted until Persia changed. The peace of Christ reconciles both Jew and Gentile to God through the cross, Ephesians 2:16.

Mordecai's honor is defined by what he did for others. Jesus states this as a principle: the great among His people must be servants, and He Himself gave His life 'as a ransom for many,' Matthew 20:26-28. Mordecai is a small case of the principle that exalted power is meant to serve. Christ is the complete case. He did not simply use His position to bless His people; He laid it aside and took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, before He was lifted up.

typology.type: The exile who becomes a blessing at the heart of the empire
typology.fulfillment: Mordecai is a Jew in Persia who brings good to the city where God placed him, as Jeremiah 29:7 told the exiles to do. It echoes the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his line, Genesis 12:3. The greater fulfilment is the Son of Abraham through whom the blessing reaches the nations, Galatians 3:14. Mordecai's blessing extended to a province. Christ's extends to every nation, and He does not merely live among the exiles but bears their exile.

study.christ:
The book of Esther ends without naming Christ, and this final chapter is the most modest in the book. Mordecai is not a disguised Jesus, and it would be a mistake to load every clause with a hidden meaning. What can be said, on the New Testament's own terms, is that this chapter draws a picture of the kind of person the Messiah would fully be, and that the picture is clearest by comparison and by contrast.

The comparison begins with the shape of Mordecai's story. He sits at a gate, he is marked by his enemies for death, and after a hidden reversal he is raised to the second seat of the empire. The fulfilment of that shape is the exaltation of the Son, who humbled Himself to death on a cross and whom God 'exalted to the highest place,' Philippians 2:8-9. Peter's sermon says He has been exalted to the right hand of God, Acts 2:33. Mordecai's exaltation was for his people's good, and so is Christ's: the Father exalted Him so that He might give the Spirit and gather every nation.

The comparison goes on with what Mordecai seeks and says. He seeks the good of his people and speaks peace to all his seed. Christ is the one who 'came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near,' Ephesians 2:17, having made the two groups one in Himself, and He is the Prince of Peace, Isaiah 9:6. He is also the one who speaks peace: 'Peace I leave with you,' John 14:27, the very promise Psalm 85:8 gave, that God would speak peace to His people.

The contrasts are as important as the comparisons. Mordecai was second to a king whose favor could change. Christ is Lord of all. Mordecai used his power to preserve a people in a foreign land for a season. Christ used His to give His life, and Jesus told His disciples that whoever wants to be great must serve, since He came not to be served but to give His life as a ransom for many, Matthew 20:26-28. The peace Mordecai spoke lasted as long as the empire. The peace of Christ is peace with God.

There is also a connecting thread that the New Testament makes explicit. Esther ends with the survival of the Jews, and the promise of Genesis 3:15 and Genesis 12:3 depended on that survival. The seed through whom the world will be blessed was preserved in exile, and Paul says that the seed is Christ, Galatians 3:16. In that sense the book ends with the seed spoken of in its last word, the offspring of Abraham, kept safe.
study.god:
The book ends by keeping God's name out of the last line, and it is right to ask what the last three verses say about Him nonetheless. They say, first, that He keeps His promises without needing to be quoted. The seed of Abraham, marked for extinction in chapter 3, now lives in peace under a foreign crown. The threats have been answered. The sentence has been reversed. And a man once forgotten in a record book is now written into it in glory. The One who ruled over a sleepless night in chapter 6 is now the One who rules over the calm that follows.

They say, second, that He works patiently through ordinary offices. There is no miracle here, no burning bush, no parted sea. There is a tax notice, a chronicle, a royal appointment and a good man doing his work. The Bible elsewhere says the LORD gives kingdoms to whom He wishes and sets up the lowly, and this is a quiet instance. He places Mordecai as He placed Joseph, Daniel and Nehemiah, in the centre of foreign power so that His people may be kept.

They say, third, that He is a God who cares about the shape of a life and not only its rescue. The book describes Mordecai's greatness in terms of what he did with it. That is a moral commendation, and it carries God's own values. In Micah 6:8 God says what He requires: to act justly, to love mercy and to walk humbly. In Psalm 34:14 God calls His people to turn from evil, do good, and seek peace and pursue it. Mordecai's last line lines up with these. God is the one who has taught, in His law, that greatness is service.

There is also a tension the ending holds. The book leaves God unnamed, and it leaves His people in Susa. He has not yet brought them home in the story, and the promises of restoration in the prophets are still waiting. The reader is asked to keep believing that a God who delivered them from Haman will bring them the rest of the way. The book's reticence about God reminds us that faith often lives in the stretch between a deliverance and its completion.

For worship, the chapter says that God's people should honor Him by the use they make of what they receive. Every gift of influence, wealth or position is a trust. The goal is the good of others, and the manner is peace. And because the ending is quiet, it teaches the worshipper to notice God's hand in the calm after the storm as well as in the storm itself.

crossReferences.note: The book begins with the king's display of 'the magnificent splendor of his greatness.' In the Hebrew the honor and greatness words used there are the same two that fall on the Jews in 8:16 and on Mordecai in 10:2-3. The book opens by admiring a king's glory and closes by giving that glory to a servant.

Mordecai exposed Bigthan and Teresh, and the deed was entered in the Book of the Chronicles and forgotten. That unrewarded entry is what the king has read to him in 6:1, and it is the first thread of the reward that 10:2 completes. A faithful act, however long unnoticed, is not lost.

Haman boasts of the honors and the promotion the king had given him. The verb used of Haman's elevation is the one used of Mordecai in 10:2. Placing the two verses next to each other shows that the same king can raise two men to the same height, and that what matters is what each does there.

A sleepless king has the chronicle read and finds that Mordecai has received nothing. The book of records that seemed a dull archive becomes the hinge of the whole story. Esther 10:2 returns to the same archive to close the story, so that the record that once condemned the king's neglect now celebrates Mordecai's greatness.

Pharaoh's ring, robe and second chariot for Joseph are the model for Mordecai's honors. Joseph too was a foreigner raised at the last moment to save many lives, and he too used his position for the good of his own people, Genesis 50:20. Mordecai's ending echoes Joseph's on Persian ground.

The prophet tells the exiles to seek the prosperity of the city where God had sent them, and to pray for it. Mordecai lives that instruction in the most public way possible. He seeks the good of everyone he can reach, and the book's last line is his reward.

The pilgrim says 'for the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, Peace be within you,' and 'I will seek your prosperity.' The two actions, speaking peace and seeking good, are those the last verse of Esther attributes to Mordecai. They are the classic marks of a servant of God's people.

Israel is told not to seek peace or prosperity from the Ammonites and Moabites. The vocabulary of seeking peace and good is the Torah's shorthand for the care a community owes its friends. Esther 10:3 turns it to a positive use: Mordecai seeks those very things for all of his own.

Jesus says the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over others, but 'whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant.' He Himself came to serve and to give His life as a ransom. Mordecai's greatness is measured by service in the way Jesus teaches, though he is only a shadow of the one who taught it.

The prophet names the promised child 'Prince of Peace,' who will bear the government on His shoulders. Mordecai's speaking of peace to all his people is a small earthly portrait of the one who will fully be what the title says.

Christ is Himself our peace, makes two groups one, reconciles both to God through the cross, and preaches peace to those far and near. This is Mordecai's last line at cosmic scale: the mediator speaks peace to all who belong to him, near and far.

God exalted Christ to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names. Mordecai's elevation in Susa is the small, provisional version of an exaltation that will be universal and permanent, when every knee bows and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord.

study.oneStory:
The story of Scripture opens with a garden where God is present and people are given work to do. When the garden is lost, the story becomes a story of a people in the wrong place, first east of Eden and then in Egypt, in the wilderness, and finally in exile. The last pages of Esther belong to the longest of those displacements. Israel is scattered across an empire that does not know God, and the question hangs over the exile: does the promise still hold?

Esther 10 gives a quiet answer. The promised seed has survived, and it has survived with a leader who seeks its good. The three verses do not close the story. There is still no temple, no king of David's line and no return of glory. What the chapter gives is a pause in the middle of the road, a proof that God's covenant people have not been erased, and a model of how to live while waiting: seek the good of the people, speak peace, and use whatever power you are given for others.

The theme then runs to Christ. Mordecai's rise, from the gate to the second seat, is a small type of the Son's descent and exaltation, Philippians 2:5-11. The exiled seed that Esther preserves becomes, in Paul's reading, the one seed of Abraham who is Christ, Galatians 3:16, through whom the blessing promised in Genesis 12:3 reaches all nations. The peace that Mordecai spoke to his kin is spoken by Christ to those far and near, Ephesians 2:17. And the greatness Mordecai showed is taught by the Lord as the rule of His kingdom, Matthew 20:26-28.

The church now lives as Mordecai's people did, among the empires, seeking the good of the city, Jeremiah 29:7, praying for it, and waiting for a homeland not yet visible. The instruction of the book applies directly. Live peacefully, serve, be honest in your work, and know that the God who is unnamed in Esther is working in the background.

The story ends in a city. In the new creation there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, the throne of God and of the Lamb is at the centre, and the nations bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24-26. The exile is over, the peace is complete, and the Servant who was greater than Mordecai reigns forever and speaks peace to all His seed.

sermon.title: Mordecai Was Great
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in Esther, this closing message expounds Esther 10:1-3, the greatness of Mordecai, showing how his partial and temporary deliverance foreshadows the complete and eternal deliverance secured in Christ. A faithful, expository handling of this movement.

quiz.q: How is Mordecai's position described at the end of the book?

options.text: Second only to King Xerxes, his deeds recorded in the royal chronicles.
options.note: Esther 10:2-3 place Mordecai second in the empire with his acts in the annals.

options.text: King over a restored Jewish kingdom in Jerusalem.
options.note: He was great in Persia, not king in Jerusalem; the book ends in exile.

options.text: A quiet elder who withdrew from public life.
options.note: The opposite: he rose to the second seat of the empire and used it publicly.

options.text: A prophet who received visions from God.
options.note: Mordecai is a statesman, not a prophet; God is never even named.

quiz.q: How does the book define Mordecai's true greatness?

options.text: By his seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his kindred.
options.note: Esther 10:3 measures greatness by the good and peace he pursued.

options.text: By the size of the tribute the king collected.
options.note: The tribute frames the empire's peace, but Mordecai's greatness is his service to his people.

options.text: By the wealth he accumulated from Haman's estate.
options.note: His estate is mentioned earlier; the closing measure of greatness is the good he sought.

options.text: By the number of enemies he destroyed.
options.note: The final verse defines his greatness by good and peace, not by conquest.

quiz.q: Which earlier biblical figure does Mordecai's rise most clearly echo?

options.text: Joseph, the lowly exile raised to be second in Egypt to save his people.
options.note: Genesis 41 sets the pattern of the faithful exile exalted to bless his people.

options.text: Moses, who led the people out of Egypt.
options.note: Both are deliverers, but the specific pattern of exile exalted to second place fits Joseph.
Mordecai is a statesman in exile, not an anointed king like David.

options.text: Elijah, the prophet who confronted kings.
options.note: Mordecai is no prophet; the echo is Joseph, the exile raised to save his people.

quiz.q: How does Mordecai's greatness point forward to Christ?

options.text: The lowly servant exalted to seek the good and speak the peace of his people foreshadows the exalted Christ, our peace.
options.note: Philippians 2:9 and Ephesians 2:14-17 fulfill the pattern in Christ.

options.text: Mordecai's earthly power is itself the salvation the Bible promises.
options.note: His deliverance was partial and passing; Christ's is complete and eternal.

options.text: Mordecai is presented as sinless and divine.
options.note: Mordecai is a flawed human servant; only Christ is God come to save.

options.text: The ending has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: The exalted servant seeking his people's good and peace runs straight to Christ.

questions: Mordecai's greatness was measured not by his rank but by his seeking the good of others. How would your own definition of a successful life change if you measured it the way this verse does?
The once-lowly man in sackcloth ended as second in the empire, yet spent his power serving his people. Where has God given you influence, and how are you using it for the good of others?

The book ends in exile, far from Jerusalem, with God still unnamed, yet plainly at work. Where do you need to trust that God is caring for you even in a season that feels far from home and empty of obvious signs?
Mordecai spoke peace to all his kindred. Who in your life is God calling you to be a peace-speaker toward this week?
Mordecai's deliverance was real but partial, a shadow of the complete rescue in Christ. How does looking past every earthly deliverer to Jesus steady your hope when human help falls short?

translationNotes.note: The greatness to which the king had raised him renders the Hebrew gedullah; the same honor Haman once craved for himself now rests on Mordecai, and it is granted, not seized.
Seeking the good and speaking peace render tov and shalom; together they define true greatness by the welfare and wholeness a ruler pursues for his people.
The closing formula echoes the exilic calling of Jeremiah 29:7 to seek the welfare of the city, and sets Mordecai in the line of Joseph and Daniel, faithful exiles raised to bless God's people.
